title: Whoa! Watch China's Space Station Zip Across the Moon!
summary: Have you ever tried to take a picture of something moving super fast? Now imagine that thing is a space station the size of a football field, zooming 250 miles above Earth, and you have less than a second to snap it crossing the Moon! That's exactly what astrophotographer Efrain Morales did on May 29. From Puerto Rico, he used a powerful 12-inch telescope and a special camera to record China's Tiangong space station as its silhouette zipped right over Tycho Crater—a huge 53-mile-wide dent on the Moon's surface. 'It is a challenge in less than a second to capture this event,' Morales said. He used a computer program called ISS Transit Finder to predict exactly when and where the station would appear. In the video, you can clearly see the station's long solar panels and its living modules. Tiangong means 'Heavenly Palace' in Chinese, and it's currently home to three taikonauts (Chinese astronauts) who arrived on May 24. The footage also shows dark patches on the Moon called 'seas'—but they're not filled with water! They're ancient lava plains with cool names like the Sea of Clouds and the Sea of Nectar. Want to spot Tiangong yourself? You can use apps to track it, just like Morales did. With a good camera and some patience, you might capture your own space station transit. Who knows—maybe you'll catch it crossing the Sun next time!
why_it_matters: Photographing space stations reminds us that people are living and working in orbit, and you can track them with just a smartphone app.

background_read: China's Tiangong space station (which means 'Heavenly Palace') has been orbiting Earth since 2021 and is home to crews of taikonauts.
Efrain Morales (an astrophotographer from Puerto Rico) used a special computer program called ISS Transit Finder to predict exactly when the station would pass in front of the Moon.
Tycho Crater is one of the Moon's most famous features, easily seen with binoculars, and was formed by a huge asteroid impact millions of years ago.
Article_Structure: WHO: Efrain Morales, an astrophotographer from Puerto Rico.
WHAT: Photographing China's Tiangong space station as it transited the Moon.
WHERE: Over the Moon, captured from Earth using a 12-inch telescope in Puerto Rico.
WHY: To capture a rare and split-second event that shows the space station's details.

perspectives.description: Amateur photographers like Morales help the world see space stations up close, making space exploration feel personal and exciting.
Some worry that the growing number of satellites and space stations might cause light pollution or clutter in orbit.
Tracking transit events teaches us about orbits and timing, blending math, technology, and artistic photography.
